1:
The word holy in the address is read two ways, and the disagreement matters. Clarke takes it strictly as consecrated, noting that Israel is called a holy people in numberless places where the people were very unholy, and warns that failing to distinguish actual holiness from the call to it has been the origin of Antinomianism, with its imputed righteousness for unholy believers whose lives are a scandal to the gospel. Calvin agrees, glossing the term as set apart and adopted, not spiritually holy, the same sense the word saints carries at the head of the epistles. Henry takes the opposite view, that these are holy not only in profession and title but in principle and practice, in heart and life, and turns aside to answer those who make the phrase a term of scorn, warning that it is dangerous jesting with such edge-tools. On the second title all agree. Robertson observes that both the phrase for holy brethren and the phrase for a heavenly calling occur only here in the New Testament, that the word for partakers is the one used of partners in the fishing, and that the call comes from heaven and is to heaven in its appeal.

That this is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an Apostle is noted by Calvin, Ellicott and Robertson alike, and each draws something different from it. Calvin takes the title as designed for the comparison at hand, since Moses is repeatedly said to have been sent by God, so that both may rightly be called messengers; and he observes that the two offices divided between Moses the teacher and Aaron the priest are here joined in one person. Ellicott finds little difference between Apostle and Prophet so applied, except that the one throws the mission into relief and the other the office, and reports that the best manuscripts omit the name Christ from the clause, leaving the personal name alone. Robertson brings in Moffatt's note that the Greek word is the Ionic equivalent of a term meaning not a mere envoy but an ambassador sent with powers, and traces the word for confession through the epistle as a recurring call to fidelity. Ellicott quotes Bengel for the antithesis the two titles make, that as Apostle he pleads the cause of God with us and as High Priest he pleads our cause with God; Wesley compresses both into the single word Mediator.

The verb rendered appointed is literally made, and it has been pressed into service by an old reading the commentators here reject. Ellicott reports that Ambrose and other Latin fathers, and apparently Athanasius as well, understood it of the creation of the human nature, and prefers instead the sentence in Samuel that it is the Lord who made Moses and Aaron; Robertson cites the same passage without argument. Gill blocks the christological reading from the other side, allowing that Christ as man was made but not as God, and holding that the apostle is speaking here not of the divine nature but of the offices, so that the phrase covers the eternal appointment, the promise, the mission and the declaration at the session on high. Clarke turns to the verse in Numbers that the comparison rests on, and supplies a sense several Jewish writers give the Hebrew word for faithful, one to whom secrets are confided with the utmost confidence of their being conscientiously kept. Robertson notes that no depreciatory remark about Moses is made anywhere in the argument, only a cheerful admission that he was faithful in all the house; Calvin insists the house is God's and not his own.
3:
The comparison turns on a builder and his building, and Robertson gives it a modern illustration, that the architect is superior to the house just as Sir Christopher Wren is superior to St Paul's Cathedral. Ellicott is careful about what the sentence actually claims, noting it is not said that Jesus is the builder but only that the relation in which he stands to the builder is set against the relation of Moses to the house, and complaining that the English word builded is unhappy, the sense being rather one who prepared or formed the house with all its necessary parts. Clarke reads it more directly, that the house is the church of God, built by Christ who is its head and governor, while Moses never put a stone in this spiritual building and was himself put into it by the architect. Calvin makes the same point as one of two arguments, that Moses so ruled the church as to remain a part and member of it, whereas the builder is superior to the whole building, and notes that the metaphor is a frequent one, so that the faithful are called living stones and even the vessels with which the house is furnished. Gill supplies what the rabbis said in Moses' praise.

The fourth verse is the acknowledged difficulty. Barnes says plainly that the words are clear and the sentiment clear, and that the only trouble is seeing what the verse is for, since if it were omitted altogether and the fifth read straight on from the third nothing would be wanting to complete the comparison; his solution is that every dispensation must have a founder, so that one person stands over both the old and the new. Ellicott agrees the parts are simple and the reasoning hard to follow with certainty, and expands the second clause as meaning that he who built this house is he who built all things, God. Clarke narrows the reference, holding that the words about all things are not about the universe at large but about the two churches, Jewish and Christian, since men may found civil and religious communities but God alone can build his own church. Calvin takes the same restriction, that although the words might be extended to the creation of the whole world he confines them to the subject in hand, namely that nothing is done in the church which ought not to be ascribed to God's power, the instrument derogating nothing from the workman. Wesley reads the inference as a direct claim to deity.

Robertson calls the antithesis of the last two verses neat and quite conclusive, since the difference between servant and son is reinforced by the difference between being in the house and being over it. Ellicott notes the word for servant is not the ordinary one and appears nowhere else in the New Testament, the translators of the Greek Old Testament having apparently felt that bond-servant suited the passage in Numbers less well than attendant or minister. Clarke rests a good deal on a breathing, observing that the pronoun unaspirated means simply his and aspirated means his own, so that on the first reading the house is God's and on the second Christ's, and that editions differ. Barnes puts the contrast in plain terms, that a servant owns nothing, inherits nothing and has no right to control anything, while a son is looked up to by all and entrusted with the whole. Calvin adds a second difference, that Moses had a doctrine committed to him which he too had to submit to. On the closing condition Robertson observes that this note of contingency runs through the whole epistle, and that no attempt is made to reconcile the warning with election, since it is wavering Christians and not God who are being exhorted.
7:
Where the sentence beginning with Wherefore actually lands is disputed and admitted to be hard. Ellicott gives the fullest account, allowing that the writer may have merged his own exhortation into the quotation and disposing of the objection that a connective would then be needed at the twelfth verse, but leaning the other way for the greater regularity of structure and because a writer of such manifest tenderness would hardly adopt so stringent a general command as his own. Calvin holds that the discourse is suspended until the twelfth verse and that the rest should be read as a parenthesis, though his own editor notes that Beza, Doddridge, Macknight and Stuart decline the parenthesis and join the word to the prohibition instead, which he thinks more suitable. Robertson takes that side without much hesitation. On the formula of citation Barnes and Clarke both find proof that the psalmist wrote by inspiration, since what David wrote is here attributed to the Holy Ghost; Robertson notes that the exact phrase occurs nowhere else in the New Testament except once in Acts. Clarke uses the passage for a longer argument, that these words and others like them imply the real possibility of falling away and would otherwise have neither sense nor meaning.

On the hardening itself Calvin is careful to keep two things together that look opposed. Our rebellion flows from no fountain but wilful wickedness, so that the unbelieving are the teachers and authors of their own perverseness and can throw the blame on nobody else; and yet it is absurd to conclude from this that we have a free power to form the heart for God's service, since we have a heart of stone by nature and shall never cease resisting until another is given us from heaven. Gill distinguishes three kinds, the natural hardness common to all, the acquired and habitual kind reached by stages from pleasing thoughts of sin to open glorying in it, and a hardness God's own people are liable to through neglect of worship and bad company. Barnes notes it works two ways, since the refusal to listen hardens of itself and men must also work at it deliberately, resisting the truth and inventing excuses. On the place named in the warning, Ellicott observes that two Hebrew proper names have been rendered by their meanings, and remarks that the rebellions they record belonged to the beginning and to the close of the wandering; Robertson notes the Greek word for the embittering is found only here and in the Greek Old Testament.

A small word decides a chronological problem. Clarke argues that the relative should be rendered where rather than when, since when implies the fathers had already seen God's works for forty years at the moment of the provocation, contrary to a history that puts the bitter provocation in the third year after the exodus; he reports the older English versions reading where, and quotes his own manuscript Bible. Robertson and Ellicott agree, Ellicott adding that the better manuscripts give where or wherewith. Where the forty years belong is a second question: Ellicott notes that in the Psalm, and apparently later in this chapter, the span attaches to what follows, while here it attaches to the provocations, and reports the opinion that it points to the interval between the ministry and the destruction of Jerusalem, with a Jewish tradition assigning forty years to the days of Messiah. Chrysostom, working further back, distinguishes three rests in the argument, the sabbath in which God rested from his works, Palestine where the people would rest from their hardships, and the kingdom of heaven which is rest indeed. Calvin keeps the middle sense, that the land promised to Abraham's seed was called rest because nowhere can we have a settled dwelling except where God fixes us.
12:
The phrase an evil heart of unbelief is a Hebrew construction that all of them unpack the same way and then read differently. Barnes and Calvin both treat the second noun as doing the work of an adjective, so that the sense is an unbelieving heart; Calvin's point is that the wickedness comes first and the unbelief follows from it, and he keeps the harsher word deliberately rather than softening it, since after men have received the knowledge of Christ their departure from the faith is not mere doubt but perfidy. Robertson calls the combination remarkable, noting that heart occurs about a thousand times in the Greek Old Testament while an evil heart appears only twice, and that the noun here means not so much unbelief as disbelief, a refusal to believe which is no mark of intelligence then or now. Ellicott points to the exact contrast the word makes with the epithet faithful applied earlier to Jesus and Moses, and notes it combines unbelief with faithlessness. On the participle Calvin's editor reports Grotius distinguishing two kinds of unbelief, the rejection of truth first offered and the renouncing of it after profession, of which the second is the more heinous.

Clarke sets out the fall as a sequence of five stages: consenting to sin under its solicitation, hardness of heart through giving way to it, unbelief following from that hardness so that the truth of the gospel is itself called in question, evil speaking against the gospel and the provision made for salvation, and finally the falling away, which extinguishes what light remained and leaves a seared conscience. Calvin describes the same descent as a matter of degrees rather than a single act, since we do not fall at the first assault into open striving against God, but are accosted artfully by indirect means until we are held in the snare, and only then break out into rebellion. Both therefore make the same practical inference, that the man who gives the least way is in danger. Barnes turns the warning into a running parallel with the wilderness, that these readers too are travelling through a barren waste, exposed to trials, surrounded by proofs of almighty power, seeking a land of rest, and that disobedience will exclude them as certainly as it excluded the fathers. Ellicott presses the epithet living, since the God whose voice they heard is watchful in warning and equally sure in punishment.

The remedy prescribed is mutual exhortation, and Calvin explains why it is needed at all: we are inclined to evil by nature and want various helps to keep us in the fear of God, since unless faith is now and then raised up it will lie prostrate, unless warmed it will freeze, unless roused it will grow torpid. Barnes takes the duty as laid on the members rather than the ministers and works out where it falls in practice, on intimate friends within the church, on parents over their children, on teachers, since a pastor can seldom see the members of his flock in private. Clarke observes that the injunction presupposes a settled state of church fellowship, without which they could have no access to one another, and adds the grim counter-example that the fathers had exhorted one another too, saying let us make a captain and return to Egypt. On the deceitfulness Ellicott personifies sin as the deceiver, luring men away either by offering pleasures or by persuading them that forbearance and respite mean there is no living God; Calvin's editor locates the particular deceit here in the present prospect of relief from persecution, since any sin deceives by some immediate gratification.
14:
Made partakers of Christ is read by everyone as union, but they measure it differently. Barnes reaches for a figure to fix what kind of union it is: the branch to the vine, which is supported and nourished by it, not the ivy and the oak, where the ivy has its own roots and merely clings and climbs; and he lists what the union involves, feeling, affection, principle, dependence and love, with nothing imparted by us and everything gained. Gill parses it as three unions at once, conjugal, so that there is communion of names, persons, goods and honour; federal, so that sin is not imputed; and that of head and members, from which come life, grace and perseverance. Robertson insists on the tense, that the verb is a perfect and means we have become partners rather than simply that we are, and that this is the reason given why they should not be tricked into apostasy. Henry keeps to the plain statement, that they are interested in all Christ is and in all he has done or will do. Wesley reads the conditional clause as a warning in disguise, since a supposition made by the Holy Ghost is equal to the strongest assertion.

The word rendered confidence is not the one used earlier in the chapter, and Ellicott marks the difference: the first meant boldness, while this is applied to men who make a firm stand when attacked and hold their ground under pressure. Clarke reaches the same sense from the etymology, that the compound means properly a basis or foundation, something on which another thing is built and by which it is supported, so that their faith was the foundation on which all their peace and salvation were raised. Calvin explains the danger the condition is aimed at, that many having only tasted the gospel think of no progress as though they had reached the summit, and so stop not merely in the middle of the race but almost at the starting-posts, and then turn another way; his answer is that Christ has given himself to be enjoyed on this condition, that the same faith which admitted us into a participation should preserve so great a blessing until death. Robertson makes the point sharper by recalling that Jonathan Edwards once said the sure proof of election is that a man holds out to the end, and by asking what has become of the loud confidence with which these readers began.

Where the repeated quotation belongs is the last structural question of the chapter, and it is left open. Ellicott judges the connection not easily decided, reporting that many join the words to what follows and begin a new paragraph but finding that improbable, and offering instead either that the previous verse is parenthetical so that this one presses the word today, or that the confidence is to be held fast precisely in the presence of a warning renewed day by day. Robertson attaches it to the holding fast while allowing it could be joined to the exhortation two verses earlier if the intervening verse is read as a parenthesis. Calvin's editor sets out the whole array, that most connect it with what precedes, as Beza, Doddridge and Macknight do, while modern authors treat it as the opening of a new paragraph, one of them confining the quotation to the first clause and giving the rest to the writer himself. Calvin's own use of the repetition is simpler: the reason for making progress never ceases while we live, because God calls us daily, and since preaching continues through the whole course of life, faith ought to continue growing with it.
16:
An accent decides the sense of the sixteenth verse, and the decision splits the commentators. Read one way the word means some, read the other it is the interrogative who, so that the sentence becomes a question answered by another question: who were they that provoked, and was it not all who came out of Egypt? Ellicott notes the oldest manuscripts give no evidence on accentuation and leave the judgment free, credits Bengel with first recovering the interrogative in modern times, and adds that an ancient Syriac version and at least three Greek fathers had it already. Clarke and Barnes both report the same list of supporters and both observe that everything down to the eighteenth verse is then a series of questions; Robertson calls the reading clearly interrogative and cites Moffatt for the answering of one rhetorical question by another as a favourite device of the diatribe style. Calvin builds on the reading the others reject, taking some as deliberately softening what David had said more severely, since a few who truly feared God were mingled with the wicked; on his view the milder word both avoids offence and sets before the readers other fathers whose faith they may imitate.

The exceptions are handled briskly by those who take the question. Clarke allows that all may be used with propriety when out of many hundreds of thousands only two were found faithful; Ellicott says the two are left out of account in the presence of the multitude of rebels; Robertson simply notes that a faithful minority existed. On the word rendered carcases, three of them agree that it means limbs rather than bodies. Ellicott takes it from the Greek of Numbers and thinks it meant to convey bodies falling limb from limb in the wilderness; Clarke, giving the same sense, hears an allusion to the scattered bleached bones long apparent there as a standing proof of the crimes and the judgment. Clarke also passes on a suggestion of Surenhusius that the forty years elegantly alludes to the time between the ascension and the writing of this epistle, then concedes at once that the dates do not quite agree, and falls back on the analogy of crime and punishment. Ellicott traces the escalation running through these four verses, since those with whom God was angry had provoked him, had sinned, had disobeyed, and had refused to believe his word.

Robertson calls the last verse the triumphant conclusion of the whole exposition of the Psalm. Ellicott declines to read it as a general summary, holding that since the oath of exclusion has just been named this sentence records the fact and states the cause in the form most useful for the exhortation in hand; and he finds force in the words could not enter, since from unbelief sprang not only disobedience but cowardice and weakness. Clarke presses the negative from the other side, that no decree of God prevented them, no necessary strength was wanting, no counsel to instruct them was deficient, since they had all these in abundance and simply chose to sin; on his account unbelief produced disobedience, disobedience produced hardness of heart and blindness of mind, and these drew down the judgments. Calvin agrees that unbelief was the primary cause though it is named last, and traces the sequence forward instead: having once rejected the possession offered them they pursued their own obstinacy, lusting, then murmuring, then in adultery and heathen superstition, so that every later sin flowed from the same fountain. Barnes measures the cost, a whole generation of many hundred thousand souls excluded from a land they had desired.
